title: Custom Labeled Pin Map: Your Names on the Map
description: Build a Custom Labeled Pin Map in the browser — drop pins, write your own labels, and capture the result for slides, guides and handouts. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a walking-tour guide pins six stops on a Custom Labeled Pin Map, names them in visiting order, and the screenshot becomes page one of the handout.
quick_answer: The Custom Labeled Pin Map lets you drop pins on a map and write your own label for each one — no account, nothing saved on a server. Build the labelled view in your browser, then capture it for slides, guides and handouts exactly as arranged.

faq: How do I capture the finished map?
Use the Map PNG Export tool or a screenshot once your labels sit where you want them — what you see is the deliverable, so zoom and pan to the final framing first.
Can I edit a label after placing the pin?
Yes — select the pin and revise its text; the map you capture reflects the latest wording. Nothing is locked until you export.
How many pins can I add?
There is no account tier counting your pins; practical limits are readability. Past a few dozen labels, switch to a legend-driven map or split the map by theme.
Can I import pins from a spreadsheet?
For bulk pins with coordinates, CSV to Map is the import route — then label the important ones here. Hand-placing suits dozens, not thousands.
Will my labels show if I share the link?
Where the tool offers a share link, the labels travel in the URL itself. Treat that link as the document: anyone with it sees the labels, so do not label anything private.
Can I use my own pin colours?
Colour choices are deliberately simple so labels stay readable. If colour-coding by category is the point, the Map with Legend tool organises entries with swatches instead.
Does it work for a printed poster?
Capture at the largest framing and check the PNG's resolution before sending it to a print shop — screen-perfect can still be print-soft at poster size.
What basemap sits under my labels?
A standard open street map (OpenStreetMap data). Your labels are the personal layer; the streets underneath stay neutral so the handout ages well.
